name: Pallid Blue-Violet
lede: Pallid Blue-Violet is a very light lavender-blue, the pallid tone Robert Ridgway charted for the base hue blue-violet in his 1912 color atlas, and close enough to Pale periwinkle to be used as its alternate name in some sources.

sections.title: A pallid tone of Blue-Violet
sections.body:
Pallid Blue-Violet puts Ridgway's tone word Pallid, meaning paler and more washed out than his plain Pale, in front of the base hue [[blue-violet]], the paired-tone method his 1912 *Color Standards and Color Nomenclature* used across the atlas [1]. The name later reached the ISCC-NBS dictionary of 1955, which filed it alongside the family's other tones [1]. Some library sources list Pallid Blue-Violet as an alternate name for [[pale-periwinkle]], a color 3.6 units away, the two sitting close enough on screen to be used almost interchangeably [1].

Its nearest distinct named neighbor is [[wedgwood-blue]], 3.7 units away and almost the same color [1]; [[lavender-blue]] sits 4.5 units out, more vivid [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Our archive finds this color in 24 of 23,781 paintings, 0.1 percent, as photographed; narrowing to at least five percent coverage inside a painting leaves 17, rarer than 63 percent of the named colors in our library [2]. It is slightly below its expected rate in the 1800s, present in 0.1 percent of the 8,345 paintings from that century, 0.8 times the archive's overall rate [2]. Inside a painting it most often plays a hidden color, in 53 percent of its 17 appearances by lightness rank, so it tends to sit in shadow or along an edge rather than out in the open [2].

The earliest match dates to 1474, in a work by Piero della Francesca, a floor and not a first since the archive's early centuries are thin; that is 438 years before the name's 1912 record, so the match marks a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, not a surviving pigment [2].
